Kamala Harris Is Campaigning Again, This Time With Abdul El-Sayed
 
Plus, Trump dismisses Iran war’s political price for GOP, and RFK Jr.’s beefed-up security is funded with money from minority-health office
 
 
DAVID GURALNICK/PRESS POOL
 

Good morning. She was the vice president in an administration that still divides Democrats.

 

She lost an election that led to a civil war within the Democratic Party. 

 

But there Kamala Harris was in Detroit on Tuesday, campaigning alongside Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the U.S. Senate in Michigan.

 

“The United States Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration, and I would suggest to you that this fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected,” Harris said, referring to El-Sayed.

 

For Harris, who some polls indicate is the leading 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, this is a relatively rare 2026 campaign stop (she has more stops coming up, including with Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia). She did briefly take a question from reporters about President Trump’s decision to remove several news outlets from the press pool, calling it “abhorrent.”

 

Other Democratic candidates haven’t exactly been clamoring for her endorsement (in fact, a bit of the opposite). Harris performed well with Black voters in 2024 though, and her support could be vital for El-Sayed in Michigan. So there she was. Is there more campaigning in her future? If she helps El-Sayed, could she help others?

 

The campaign of El-Sayed’s rival, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, painted Harris’s appearance as a sign of desperation.

 

Democrats are torn. They are trying to project a new vision and new candidates to take the country into 2027 and beyond. Harris is tied to the unpopular former President Joe Biden, and she had plenty of missteps of her own in 2024. But she is still one of the party’s most recognizable figures, and Ossoff’s support of her certainly matters. Will Democratic voters follow Harris’s lead in 2026? What about in 2027 and 2028?

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Volodymyr Zelensky: Ukraine’s president said he has asked Trump for a “winter package” of military equipment, including Patriot antimissile systems.

 

Xi Jinping: China’s leader is arriving in Washington for a state visit, following weekslong talks over the trip’s designation.

 

Trump’s Wednesday: The president is scheduled to hold policy meetings from 11 a.m. ET to 3:30 p.m. Then at 6 p.m., he will greet Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at Joint Base Andrews, ahead of their visit to the White House.

What I’m Following

 
 
BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/PRESS POOL
 

Trump didn’t seem fazed about the fallout of his United Nations remarks for the GOP. Less than six weeks before the midterms, the Iran war Trump defended before the General Assembly has become one of the Republican Party’s biggest vulnerabilities. The president argued that his most important mission is preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, and that the political price was a small one to pay. Takeaways from his speech.

 

HHS shifted about $12 million from its Office of Minority Health to help cover security expenses for Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The cost of security for the health secretary grew from roughly $10 million in fiscal year 2025 to $17 million in fiscal year 2026, people familiar with the matter said. The Office of Minority Health was created under former President Ronald Reagan after a landmark report found that Black infants in the U.S. were more likely than white babies to die and that Black life expectancy was shorter.

 

A GOP senator called for an investigation of Donald Trump Jr. The president’s eldest son received a lavish afterparty as a wedding gift from a Russian businessman connected to the Kremlin. Sen. John Curtis (R., Utah) requested a probe into the “use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access by domestic and foreign interests.”

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Trump said he was considering restrictions on diesel exports in a move to curb rising fuel prices.

 

• Vice President JD Vance’s antifraud task force is removing hundreds of thousands of enrollments from the Affordable Care Act’s public exchanges.

 

• Trump signed a deal with Greenland and Denmark to pave the way for a larger U.S. military presence on the Arctic island.
